headline: Captree Dock Talk: Bridge Fluke Holding Steady While Bass Hug the Inlet Seam
subhead: A sloppy ocean pushed the fleet inside this week, and the fish that matter most right now were waiting there anyway.
body_markdown:
Ran into Vinny at the fuel dock Tuesday morning, just off a half-day charter, shaking his head about the ocean. "Three-footers on a four-second period," he said, like that explains everything — and honestly, it does. That's a mean, stacked-up chop, not a rolling swell you can fish through comfortably, and it's had the open-water guys running back through the inlet by ten a.m. all week. I told him what I've been telling everybody who'll listen: quit fighting the Atlantic and go find where the fish already are. They're inside. They've been inside.

The water temp out at the buoy off the Bight is sitting around 71.6, which sounds warm and it is, but that short, choppy 3-to-4 foot slop with a southwest-leaning swell direction has made the surf and near-shore ocean grounds miserable to fish with any precision. Meanwhile the bay and the inlet channels are calm, structured, and full of bait. That's the story this week — not one big bite everywhere, but a handful of very specific, very productive windows if you know where to put the boat.

Fluke first, because that's been the most consistent thing going. The Robert Moses bridges — both the Fire Island span and the Captree side — are still holding fish in that 25 to 35 foot band along the pilings and the current breaks off the pilons. I've been drifting white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, working the last two hours of the outgoing when the current really combs bait past the structure. Doubles have come over the rail more than once when the drift lines up right — nothing giant, mostly 17 to 20 inches with a few pushing 4 pounds mixed in, but steady enough that a morning trip is worth your gas. If the current's slack or barely moving, don't bother — these fish want that pressure pushing bait to them, and dead water at the bridges is dead fishing.

Striped bass have settled into a real pattern at the inlet seam, right where the outgoing dumps out past Democrat Point and the current rips against the deeper channel edge. Bunker schools have been pushing through there on the last two hours of the ebb, and the bass are sitting underneath and behind them, picking off stragglers. I've had my best luck snagging a bunker and dropping it right into the seam, letting it sink on a fish-finder rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in that current — no need for anything fancy. Bucktail guys working the same water with 2-ounce white or bone bucktails, bounced slow along the bottom edge where the sand drops into the channel, have connected too, though the bunker-drop has been the more consistent producer. Sizes have been mixed — a lot of mid-20s to low-30s, with the occasional bigger fish mixed into the bunker pods right at first light or the last hour before dark. This isn't an all-day bite. It's tide-and-light dependent, and if you miss that window, you're just burning fuel.

Bluefish have been riding shotgun with those bunker schools at the inlet mouth, and they've actually been the more reliable action some mornings — chopper blues in the 3 to 6 pound range busting bait right on the surface off Democrat Point, visible from a hundred yards out by the birds working overhead. Simple diamond jigs or a topwater popper thrown right into the commotion has been all it takes. If you want fast, aggressive action without overthinking the tide, that's your play right now.

I'll be straight with you on weakfish — it's been quiet. A few guys working the deeper holes off Nicoll Bay after dark with soft-plastic grubs on light jig heads have picked at a fish or two, but it's nothing like the numbers we used to see this time of year in the bay, and I'm not going to sell you on a bite that isn't really there. If weakfish are your target, treat it as a bonus fish while you're doing something else, not a dedicated trip.

Porgies have been the honest, blue-collar bite this week, and I mean that as a compliment. Anchoring up on the rockpiles inside Fire Island Inlet and around Democrat Point with sandworms or clam on a simple hi-lo rig has produced steady, respectable numbers — not trophy fish, but a cooler full of dinner porgies for not much effort, which is worth something when the bigger stuff is being finicky about tide and light.

Looking ahead, the ocean forecast doesn't show that chop settling down dramatically through the weekend, so I'd keep planning around the inside game rather than fighting the surf. If the wind does back off and that swell period stretches out, Democrat Point and the ocean beaches west toward Cedar Beach could turn on for bass working bait pushed tight to the sand — that's the scenario I'd watch for. Until then, I'd fish the last two hours of the outgoing at the inlet seam for bass and bunker, hit the bridges on that same dropping water for fluke, and keep a rod rigged with a diamond jig for whatever blues show up chopping on the surface. It's not a blowout week, but it's an honest one, and there's enough happening inside that a well-timed trip should put fish in the box.
